newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FORECAST - Swedish debt yields to fall before rise.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Swedish debt yields to fall before rise.

text.p: Short and long Swedish debt yields are expected to fall in the short-term, but analysts said in the longer-term they would rise from current levels.
The crown was expected to remain stable against the mark during 1997, according to a Reuters survey.

Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, was seen further lowering its key interest rate, the repo rate, so it would stand at 3.75 percent in one year's time but bottom at 3.53 percent sometime in the first half of 1997.
The repo rate, which lies between the bank's deposit and lending rates that mark out the central bank's interest rate corridor, currently stands at 4.10 percent.

"I believe we will see mediocre growth in 1997, but that the business cycle will pick up in 1998. For this reason the repo rate will bottom in the first half of the year to be raised later," one economist told Reuters.
"There is a risk for increasing inflation because of higher growth in 1998 and since monetary policy takes time to have an effect, the Riksbank will begin to raise rates far in advance."
However, not all economists see growth picking up.
"Sweden will benefit from a strong Norway and Finland on either side," said Ian Ganna, economist at Chase.

"But on the other hand Sweden is dependent on exports and the rest of Europe is going to tighten fiscal policy in 1997, which will not benefit Sweden," Ganna said, forecasting longer interest rates would fall in the longterm as well.
On average, economists forecast the ten year bond yield to be 7.03 percent in one year, about 40 basis points above current levels.
"Gradually economies will take off, especially in Germany. Longer German yields will come up then and Swedish ones will follow," said Rikard Kull, economist at Post Giro bank.
The repo rate is also seen following this pattern. When the rate has reached bottom, the short end of the yield curve is expected to rise.
In one year the six month T-bill rate was forecast to be 4.01 percent and three month paper 3.48 percent.
In one month the six month T-bill rate is seen falling to 3.57 percent from its current level of 3.72 percent.

The crown is expected to be strong and stable against the mark in the short and long term, economists said. In three months the currency is expected to be 4.34 crowns against the mark and strengthen to 4.30 crowns in one year.
At 1330 GMT the crown was trading at 4.3625 against the mark.
"A good argument exists for a stable and strong crown versus the mark. Fundamentals are strong in Sweden and there's a big surplus in the trade balance," said Handelsbanken economist Bengt Hansson.
Sweden's trade surplus was 12.5 billion crowns in November, around one billion crowns more than market expectations and compared to 10.6 billion in November 1995.
